title: Summarization & Compaction
summary: A conversation grows until it no longer fits the context window. Summarization fixes this by compacting old turns into a compact running summary that you keep in the prompt, while recent turns stay verbatim. You trigger it on a threshold, feed the oldest messages to the model to summarize, replace them with the summary, and accept that summarization is lossy — the craft is deciding when to compact and what detail to preserve.
nestedConcepts: summarizing old turns with the model

subtopics.title: Why compaction is needed
subtopics.explanation: Every message is re-sent each call, so a long conversation eventually exceeds the context window and cost climbs the whole way there. You cannot keep everything verbatim forever, and truncating oldest-first silently drops facts the agent still needs. Compaction is the middle path — shrink the old material instead of deleting it — which is why it becomes essential the moment conversations run long.
subtopics.example:
MAX_TOKENS = 8000

# naive: keep appending forever -> eventually overflows the window
while chatting:
    history.append(next_turn())
    if count_tokens(history) > MAX_TOKENS:
        # truncating oldest-first LOSES facts the agent still needs
        # compaction is the alternative: shrink, don't delete
        history = compact(history)

subtopics.title: The rolling summary buffer
subtopics.explanation: The core structure is a buffer holding one running summary plus the most recent verbatim turns. Old turns get folded into the summary; new turns append at the tail; the middle is never kept raw for long. This rolling-summary-buffer shape is the standard pattern that keeps a conversation bounded no matter how long it runs.

subtopics.title: When to trigger summarization
subtopics.explanation: You summarize on a threshold, not every turn: commonly when token count crosses a fraction of the window, or when the recent buffer exceeds a turn count. Summarizing too eagerly wastes calls and loses detail; too late risks overflow. Choosing the trigger point is the tuning knob that balances the cost of summarizing against the risk of running out of room.
subtopics.example:
SUMMARY_TRIGGER = 6   # summarize once we exceed this many recent turns

def maybe_compact(state, summarize_fn):
    if len(state["recent"]) > SUMMARY_TRIGGER:
        # fold the oldest turns into the summary, keep the last few raw
        old = state["recent"][:-2]
        state["recent"] = state["recent"][-2:]
        state["summary"] = summarize_fn(state["summary"], old)
    return state

subtopics.title: Summarize old turns with the model
subtopics.explanation: Compaction itself is usually an LLM call: you prompt the model to fold the existing summary plus the oldest turns into a new, shorter summary that preserves decisions, facts, and open threads. A focused instruction ('keep names, numbers, and unresolved items') controls what survives. Using the model to summarize is what lets compaction preserve meaning rather than just chopping text.
subtopics.example:
def summarize_fn(prev_summary, old_turns):
    text = "\n".join(f"{m['role']}: {m['content']}" for m in old_turns)
    prompt = [
        {"role": "system", "content":
         "Update the running summary. Keep names, numbers, decisions, "
         "and any unresolved items. Be concise."},
        {"role": "user", "content":
         f"Existing summary:\n{prev_summary}\n\nNew turns:\n{text}"},
    ]
    return llm(prompt)   # returns the new, shorter running summary

subtopics.title: The lossy tradeoff
subtopics.explanation: Summarization discards detail by design, so some specifics — an exact quote, a minor aside — are gone once compacted. You mitigate this by protecting critical facts (store them as structured semantic memory), keeping recent turns verbatim, and summarizing conservatively. Accepting and managing the lossy tradeoff is what separates a compaction scheme that stays useful from one that quietly forgets what mattered.

foundations.overview: Because a conversation's full message list is re-sent every call, a long session inevitably approaches the context window's limit while cost rises the entire way. Deleting the oldest messages avoids overflow but silently loses information the agent may still need. Summarization and compaction take the middle path: periodically fold older turns into a compact running summary that stays in the prompt, while the most recent turns remain verbatim. The canonical structure is a rolling summary buffer — one summary string plus a short tail of raw recent turns. You trigger compaction on a threshold (a fraction of the window, or a recent-turn count), summarize the oldest turns with a focused LLM call that preserves decisions, names, numbers, and open threads, then replace those turns with the updated summary. The catch is that summarization is inherently lossy: fine detail is discarded by design. You manage that by pinning critical facts as structured data that bypasses summarization, keeping recent turns raw, and compacting conservatively. Done well, compaction lets a conversation run indefinitely within a bounded, affordable window.
foundations.formalDefinition: Summarization (compaction) is the operation of replacing a span of older conversation messages with a shorter generated summary that preserves salient information, maintained as a rolling summary buffer: state = (running_summary, recent_verbatim_turns). Compaction is triggered when a size threshold is exceeded and typically implemented as an LLM call that merges the prior summary with the oldest turns.
foundations.whyItMatters: Compaction is what makes long-running and multi-session agents feasible at all — without it, conversations either overflow the context window or become prohibitively expensive per turn. It is the standard, production-grade answer to unbounded history growth and a prerequisite for agents that hold hours-long or recurring conversations.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of taking meeting minutes. You don't transcribe every word forever; you keep the last few exchanges fresh in your head and periodically compress everything older into a tidy paragraph of 'here's where we are'. Important figures and action items get written on a separate, permanent sticky note so they're never lost in the summarizing — that sticky note is your pinned facts.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Long-lived chat assistants compact old turns to keep sessions affordable; coding agents summarize earlier file exploration to free room for current edits; customer-support bots roll a summary across a multi-day ticket; and research agents compress prior findings into a running brief as they gather more.
foundations.performanceImpact: Compaction trades a periodic extra summarization call for a much smaller, bounded prompt on every subsequent turn; since each turn re-sends the whole context, replacing many verbatim tokens with a short summary sharply lowers steady-state per-turn cost and latency, easily repaying the occasional summarize call.
commonUseCases: Keeping long chat sessions within the context window
Rolling a summary across a multi-day support ticket
Freeing room in coding agents after early exploration
Compressing prior findings in a research agent

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should summarize every turn to stay small.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Summarizing constantly wastes model calls and strips useful recent detail; you compact on a threshold and keep the latest turns verbatim.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Summarization is lossless if the prompt is good.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It is lossy by design — detail is discarded. Protect must-keep facts by pinning them as structured data rather than trusting the summary to retain them.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Truncating the oldest messages is basically the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Truncation deletes information outright; compaction preserves the gist of old turns in a summary, which keeps the agent coherent instead of amnesiac.

codeLab.title: Build a rolling summary buffer
codeLab.instructions: Implement compact(state, summarize_fn, keep_recent, trigger) where state is {"summary": str, "recent": list}. When len(state['recent']) > trigger, fold the oldest turns into the summary: keep the last keep_recent turns verbatim, pass the older turns to summarize_fn(prev_summary, old_turns) (which returns the new summary string), and update state in place; otherwise leave state unchanged. Return state either way. Assume trigger >= keep_recent.
codeLab.testHarness:
def summarize_fn(prev, old):
    tag = " | ".join(m["content"] for m in old)
    return (prev + " | " + tag) if prev else tag

state = {"summary": "", "recent":
         [{"role": "user", "content": f"m{i}"} for i in range(8)]}
state = compact(state, summarize_fn, keep_recent=2, trigger=6)
assert len(state["recent"]) == 2
assert [m["content"] for m in state["recent"]] == ["m6", "m7"]
assert state["summary"] == "m0 | m1 | m2 | m3 | m4 | m5"

# under trigger -> unchanged
small = {"summary": "", "recent":
         [{"role": "user", "content": f"x{i}"} for i in range(3)]}
small = compact(small, summarize_fn, keep_recent=2, trigger=6)
assert len(small["recent"]) == 3 and small["summary"] == ""
print("all tests passed")
hints: Only compact when len(state['recent']) > trigger; otherwise return state untouched.
state['recent'][:-keep_recent] is the older span to fold; state['recent'][-keep_recent:] is the tail to keep verbatim.
Assign summarize_fn(state['summary'], old) back to state['summary'] so the summary accumulates across compactions.

checkpoints.prompt: Why is compaction preferred over just truncating the oldest messages?
options: Compaction preserves the gist of old turns in a summary instead of deleting the information
Truncation isn't allowed by the API
Compaction uses fewer tokens than truncation always
checkpoints.explanation: Truncation deletes information outright, so the agent can forget facts it still needs. Compaction folds old turns into a summary, keeping the meaning while bounding size — coherent rather than amnesiac.

checkpoints.prompt: With trigger checked as > and keep_recent=2, what stays verbatim?
checkpoints.code:
recent = [f"m{i}" for i in range(5)]  # m0..m4
trigger, keep_recent = 3, 2
if len(recent) > trigger:
    old = recent[:-keep_recent]
    recent = recent[-keep_recent:]
print(recent)
checkpoints.explanation: len(recent)=5 > trigger=3, so compaction runs. recent[-2:] keeps the last two verbatim turns, ['m3', 'm4'], while m0-m2 fold into the summary.

checkpoints.prompt: This summarizer discards the running history. What's the bug?
options: prev_summary is never included, so each compaction forgets everything summarized before it
checkpoints.explanation: A rolling summary must fold new turns into the PRIOR summary. Ignoring prev_summary means every compaction only summarizes the latest batch and drops all earlier compacted history — the buffer stops rolling.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the trigger so compaction fires only when the buffer is too big.
checkpoints.codeBefore:
def maybe_compact(state, keep_recent, trigger):
    if len(state["recent"])
checkpoints.codeAfter:
trigger:
        old = state["recent"][:-keep_recent]
        state["recent"] = state["recent"][-keep_recent:]
        state["summary"] = summarize(state["summary"], old)
checkpoints.explanation: You compact only once the recent buffer has grown beyond the threshold, i.e. len(recent) > trigger. Using < or <= would summarize while the buffer is still small, wasting calls and stripping recent detail.

theory.question: What is a rolling summary buffer and why do agents use it?
theory.directAnswer: It's a memory structure holding one running summary of older turns plus a short tail of recent turns kept verbatim. Agents use it because full history is re-sent every call and eventually overflows the context window; folding old turns into a compact summary bounds the prompt size while preserving the gist, unlike truncation which deletes information.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A two-part state — (running_summary, recent_verbatim_turns) — where older messages are periodically compressed into the summary and the newest stay raw.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because the whole context is re-tokenized each turn, long conversations grow past the window and become costly; a bounded buffer keeps steady-state size and price flat.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: On a size threshold, the oldest turns beyond the recent tail are passed with the prior summary to an LLM summarization call that returns an updated summary; those turns are then replaced by the summary in the prompt, and recent turns continue appending.

theory.whyImportant: It is the standard, production-grade solution to unbounded history growth and a prerequisite for long-running or multi-session agents.
theory.realWorldExample: A multi-day support ticket keeps a rolling summary ('customer reported billing error on order A-123, refund pending') plus the last few messages, so each new agent turn stays small and affordable without losing the thread.

followUps.question: How do you avoid the summary itself growing without bound?
followUps.answer: Summarize the summary too — each compaction rewrites the prior summary more tersely — and pin only essential facts, so it converges rather than accumulates.

followUps.question: What should stay verbatim?
followUps.answer: The system prompt, pinned critical facts, and the most recent turns, since fresh detail matters most for the next response.

theory.question: Summarization is lossy. How do you decide when to summarize and how to limit what's lost?
theory.directAnswer: Trigger compaction on a size threshold — a fraction of the context window or a recent-turn count — rather than every turn, balancing summarize-call cost against overflow risk. Limit loss by keeping recent turns verbatim, instructing the summarizer to retain names, numbers, decisions, and open threads, and pinning must-keep facts as structured data that bypasses summarization entirely.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A tuning-and-mitigation problem: choosing the compaction trigger and protecting critical information from lossy compression.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Summarizing too eagerly wastes calls and strips useful detail; too late risks window overflow; and any summary discards specifics by design.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Measure prompt tokens per turn, set the trigger at a safe fraction of the limit, use a focused summarization prompt to preserve salient content, keep a verbatim recent tail, and store pinned facts separately so they are re-injected exactly every call.

theory.whyImportant: It's the difference between a compaction scheme that stays coherent and one that quietly forgets the facts that mattered, which directly affects agent reliability and cost.
theory.realWorldExample: A coding agent compacts early file-exploration turns once the prompt hits 70% of the window but pins the target file path and the failing test name as structured facts, so those are never summarized away even as the narrative is compressed.

followUps.question: Why not summarize on every single turn to stay minimal?
followUps.answer: Each summarization is an extra model call and it strips recent detail the next response often needs; threshold-based compaction is cheaper and preserves fresh context.

followUps.question: Where do pinned facts fit in the memory taxonomy?
followUps.answer: They're semantic memory — durable structured facts kept outside the lossy summary and re-injected exactly when needed.

scenario.question: After adding summarization, your agent stops overflowing the window but starts 'forgetting' specific commitments it made earlier in the chat. How do you diagnose and fix it without abandoning compaction?
scenario.directAnswer: The commitments are being lost to lossy summarization. Diagnose by inspecting the running summary at the point the fact disappears; then protect critical items by pinning them as structured facts that bypass the summary, tightening the summarizer prompt to retain decisions and open items, keeping a longer verbatim recent tail, and compacting less aggressively.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A loss-of-detail failure caused by compaction discarding specifics the agent still needs.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Summaries compress by dropping detail; commitments made in older turns get generalized away or omitted when they fall outside the verbatim tail.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Log the summary before and after each compaction to find where the fact vanishes, add a structured pinned-facts store re-injected verbatim each turn, instruct the summarizer explicitly to preserve promises/decisions/numbers, and raise keep_recent or the trigger threshold so recent commitments stay raw longer.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows summarization is a tradeoff to be engineered, not a free win, and demonstrates the standard mitigations that keep compaction reliable.
scenario.realWorldExample: A scheduling agent forgot it had promised a Thursday callback once that turn was summarized; pinning open commitments as structured facts and adding 'preserve any promises' to the summarizer prompt eliminated the regression while keeping the window bounded.

followUps.question: How would you catch this class of bug automatically?
followUps.answer: Add evals that replay long conversations and assert key facts survive compaction, alerting when a pinned or promised item is missing from the reconstructed context.

followUps.question: What's the risk of just disabling summarization?
followUps.answer: You return to unbounded growth — overflow, higher cost, and latency — so the right fix is protecting facts, not removing compaction.

coding.question: Write a function that builds the final prompt from a rolling-summary state: system message, then pinned facts, then the running summary (if any), then the recent verbatim turns, in that order.
coding.thoughtProcess: The order matters for the model: stable instructions first, then durable pinned facts, then the compressed summary as context, then the freshest raw turns last so they're most salient. I only include the summary block when it's non-empty to avoid injecting an empty line, and I copy the recent turns onto the end rather than mutating them.
lineByLine: Start with the system instructions, which must always lead the prompt.
Add pinned facts as a system message only when present, so durable data is re-injected exactly.
Include the running summary block only if non-empty to avoid a blank context line.
Append the recent verbatim turns last so the freshest content is most salient to the model.
The __main__ block assembles system + pinned + summary + one recent turn and prints each in order.
coding.timeComplexity: O(r) in the number of recent turns copied into the prompt.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(r) for the assembled message list.

followUps.question: Why put recent turns last rather than the summary?
followUps.answer: Recency and position both matter — the freshest turns are most relevant to the next reply and benefit from the salient tail position of the prompt.

followUps.question: How does this interact with the 'lost in the middle' effect?
followUps.answer: Critical pinned facts sit near the top and recent turns near the bottom; you avoid burying must-use information in the low-attention middle of the context.

keyTakeaways: Full history is re-sent every call, so long conversations overflow the window — compaction shrinks old turns instead of deleting them.
The standard structure is a rolling summary buffer: one running summary plus a short tail of recent verbatim turns.
Trigger summarization on a size threshold, not every turn, to balance summarize-call cost against overflow risk.
Compaction is lossy by design; protect must-keep information by pinning it as structured facts that bypass the summary.
Fold new turns into the PRIOR summary so the buffer keeps rolling, and keep the system prompt and recent turns verbatim.
